title: How to Manage Your Time as a First-Time Lead
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Gregor Ojstersek shares practical time management strategies for first-time engineering leads, drawing on his own unsustainable experience of 10-12+ hour workdays trying to serve simultaneously as manager and hands-on engineer. The central insight: the more senior you become, the more you succeed through others, not through your own output -- leaders who take on all the hardest tasks become bottlenecks. Five accessible strategies: (1) Prioritize ruthlessly using a four-quadrant framework (do first / schedule / delegate / don't do) and make decisions quickly -- indecision often creates more problems than a wrong decision; (2) Block focus time (2-3 hours daily) in your calendar with notifications off; (3) Use Pomodoro timer (25/5 or 50/10 minute cycles) to enforce deep work; (4) Improve communication -- overcommunication in a remote or distributed team is usually the right amount; (5) Remove pointless meetings (ask: does this help make a decision? could it be async?). Additional sections on maker vs. manager time, saying no, and taking time off were available to paid subscribers. The overall prescription: good time management is not about working faster but about protecting the conditions for doing the right work and enabling the team to do the same.
points: * The foundational shift: the more senior you become, the more you succeed through others, not through your own output -- leaders who try to take on all the hardest tasks become bottlenecks and prevent team growth. * Prioritize ruthlessly with the four-quadrant framework: do first (important + urgent), schedule (important but not urgent), delegate (urgent but less important), don't do (not urgent and not important) -- and make decisions quickly. * Block focus time (2-3 hours daily or half-day weekly) with notifications off; unprotected calendar time gets consumed by meetings and 'someone else's priorities.' * Overcommunication is usually the right amount of communication in distributed and remote teams -- say important things in a meeting AND follow up in writing, explaining the 'why' behind decisions. * Remove pointless meetings: ask whether the meeting produces a decision, whether it is necessary, or whether it could be handled asynchronously -- and don't hesitate to remove a standing meeting that no longer serves its purpose.
quotes: The more senior you become, the more you succeed through others, not through your own output.
if you don't manage your time correctly, your team will struggle, important work won't get done, and you will eventually burn out.
Indecision often creates so many more problems, in some cases, a lot more problems than making a wrong decision.
If you don't protect focused work time, your calendar gets consumed by meetings and 'someone else's priorities'.
I intentionally overcommunicate specific topics in order to ensure that things are really clear.
Overcommunication is usually the right amount of communication.
There's nothing wrong with removing a meeting that is no longer useful. Not every meeting should exist.
